Using LLM for Improving Mapping between
Enterprise Architectural Views
Walt L. Melo
MITRE Corporation
Georgetown University
George Washington University
USA
Abstract—This paper presents an AI-assisted semantic trace-
ability workflow for recommending candidate mappings between
DoDAF architectural viewpoints. The workflow uses dense se-
mantic embeddings for initial candidate retrieval through cosine
similarity, followed by cross-encoder re-ranking to refine candi-
date ordering. Candidate mappings are validated by a subject
matter expert (SME) and evaluated based on candidate coverage,
recommendation ranking, and relevance within a top-3 review
budget. The approach was evaluated on a real-world Positioning,
Navigation, and Timing (PNT) Enterprise Architecture developed
for a U.S. federal government department. Three mapping tasks
were examined: Capability-to-Operational Activity, Operational
Activity-to-Service, and Capability-to-Service. At least one SME-
validated relationship appeared within the first three recom-
mendations for 100%, 95%, and 100% of the evaluated cases,
respectively. Cross-encoder re-ranking improved the placement of
valid relationships for Operational Activity-to-Service mapping,
but the observed differences from cosine retrieval were not
statistically significant. A stricter relevance criterion reduced
the proportion of fully relevant recommendations, highlighting
the need for SME validation to distinguish complete from
partial traceability relationships. The findings support semantic
retrieval as a decision-support mechanism for cross-viewpoint
traceability while motivating further evaluation across additional
architectures, viewpoints, and domains.

I. INTRODUCTION
Modern enterprise systems engineering relies heavily on
standardized architecture frameworks, such as the Department
of Defense Architecture Framework (DoDAF) and the Unified
Architecture Framework (UAF), to model complex, multi-
domain systems. A core tenet of these frameworks is the
establishment of rigorous, cross-layer traceability between
architectural viewpoints. For instance, DoDAF advocates map-
ping Strategic Capabilities to Operational Activities to ensure

enterprise alignment, as well as mapping Operational Activi-
ties to services, systems, software, and components to verify
that physical and logical solutions fulfill required operational
functions. Establishing this inter-viewpoint alignment guaran-
tees that high-level strategic goals directly inform operational
behaviors and downstream resource implementations.
Despite its critical importance, manually establishing and
maintaining inter-viewpoint traceability matrices across large-
scale enterprise architectures is extraordinarily labor-intensive
and costly. Systems engineers frequently spend hundreds of
hours facilitating intensive review workshops with Subject
Matter Experts (SMEs) to manually validate these mappings.
As architectures expand or undergo iterative modifications,
manual tracing becomes increasingly susceptible to human
error, resulting in missing traceability links, unfulfilled op-
erational activities, or orphaned system resources.
To mitigate this bottleneck, recent developments in Large
Language Models (LLMs) and Information Retrieval (IR)
offer a promising avenue for improving mapping between
architectural views. This paper presents an AI-assisted work-
flow designed to automatically discover, rank, and recom-
mend candidate traceability links between DoDAF architec-
tural viewpoints, serving as an automated decision-support
tool for systems engineers. The workflow leverages dense
semantic embeddings generated from model element textual
descriptions to conduct initial candidate retrieval (rank-by-
cosine), followed by a cross-encoder re-ranking stage (rank-
by-rerank) to capture nuanced semantic relationships between
source and target model elements.
To evaluate the effectiveness and reliability of the generated
mappings, the proposed workflow was applied to an Position,
Navigation, and Time (PNT) enterprise architecture , modeled
in DoDAF using Cameo Systems Modeler. The automated
recommendations were validated by a SME. We demonstrated
that the workflow recovers complex architectural relation-
ships, potentially reducing engineer inspection effort.

This paper presents an AI-assisted work-
flow designed to automatically discover, rank, and recom-
mend candidate traceability links between DoDAF architec-
tural viewpoints, serving as an automated decision-support
tool for systems engineers. The workflow leverages dense
semantic embeddings generated from model element textual
descriptions to conduct initial candidate retrieval (rank-by-
cosine), followed by a cross-encoder re-ranking stage (rank-
by-rerank) to capture nuanced semantic relationships between
source and target model elements.
To evaluate the effectiveness and reliability of the generated
mappings, the proposed workflow was applied to an Position,
Navigation, and Time (PNT) enterprise architecture , modeled
in DoDAF using Cameo Systems Modeler. The automated
recommendations were validated by a SME. We demonstrated
that the workflow recovers complex architectural relation-
ships, potentially reducing engineer inspection effort. While
demonstrated on DoDAF models exported from Cameo, the
underlying workflow is tool- and framework-agnostic, making
it broadly applicable across Enterprise Architecture (EA) and
Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) domains.
The primary contributions of this paper are as follows:
• Automated Inter-Viewpoint Mapping Workflow: We
introduce a two-stage retrieval-then-reranking semantic
workflow tailored specifically for establishing traceabil-
ity across DoDAF Capability, Operational, and Service
viewpoints.
• Industrial Case Study Validation: We demonstrate
the practical utility of the workflow on a real-world,
industrial-scale DoDAF enterprise architecture developed
for a U.S. federal government department in Cameo
Systems Modeler.
• Rigorous SME Ground Truth Evaluation: A SME
validated the mappings using rank-aware Information Re-
trieval metrics to measure retrieval yield and engineering
review efficiency.
The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Sec-
tion II Related Work reviews related literature in AI-driven
traceability link recovery and synthesizes current research
gaps. Section III Technical Approach details the case study, a
six-step semantic traceability workflow used to automatically
provide link candidates between DoDAF viewpoints, and the
artificial intelligence platform (AIP) used to support this
workflow. Section IV Results presents the empirical evaluation
results, followed by conclusions and future work.
II. RELATED WORK
A. Evaluation Approach
To systematically assess AI-driven approaches for estab-
lishing links between DoDAF architectural viewpoints, we
synthesize an evaluation framework anchored in Information
Retrieval for Traceability Link Recovery (IR-TLR) protocols
[1], [2] and re-ranking paradigms.
Our comparative framework evaluates existing literature
across four core dimensions:
1) AI & Retrieval Architecture: Categorizes the under-
lying retrieval and ranking mechanisms—ranging from
classic Vector Space Models (VSM/LSI) and bi-encoder
Transformer embeddings (e.g., BERT, SimCSE) to two-
stage retrieval-then-reranking pipelines (cross-encoders
and LLM re-rankers).
2) Link Quality & Top-k IR Rigor: Evaluates candidate
recommendation quality as a top-k decision-support
task for systems engineers using rank-aware Information
Retrieval metrics (evaluated at a fixed review budget,
e.g., k = 3).
3) Architectural Interpretability & Governance: Exam-
ines the transparency of generated candidate links, eval-
uating whether the approach provides scalar similarity
scores or actionable semantic justifications suitable for
engineering review and model audits.
4) Empirical Validation & MBSE Toolchain Integra-
tion: Evaluates benchmark realism, contrasting stud-
ies validated on synthetic or static textual documents
against those using formal MBSE repository models
(e.g., Cameo Systems Modeler exports) across intercon-
nected DoDAF views.
B. Background
The establishment and maintenance of traceability links
across architectural viewpoints are essential for ensuring oper-
ational coverage, resource justification, and capability fulfill-
ment. Traditionally, maintaining consistency across DoDAF
or UAF viewpoints relied on manual inspection by SMEs.
Recent advances in Natural Language Processing (NLP), dense
semantic embeddings, and Large Language Models (LLMs)
offer automated alternatives for model-to-model alignment.
1) Transition from Keyword IR to Dense Semantic Embed-
dings: Early automated traceability approaches relied heavily
on statistical IR methods such as Term Frequency-Inverse
Document Frequency (TF-IDF) and Latent Semantic Index-
ing (LSI) [3]. While efficient, these methods struggle with
vocabulary mismatch across DoDAF viewpoints: Strategic ca-
pabilities are often expressed in high-level business terminol-
ogy, whereas Operational Activities and Services components
employ technical or domain-specific language.

B. Background
The establishment and maintenance of traceability links
across architectural viewpoints are essential for ensuring oper-
ational coverage, resource justification, and capability fulfill-
ment. Traditionally, maintaining consistency across DoDAF
or UAF viewpoints relied on manual inspection by SMEs.
Recent advances in Natural Language Processing (NLP), dense
semantic embeddings, and Large Language Models (LLMs)
offer automated alternatives for model-to-model alignment.
1) Transition from Keyword IR to Dense Semantic Embed-
dings: Early automated traceability approaches relied heavily
on statistical IR methods such as Term Frequency-Inverse
Document Frequency (TF-IDF) and Latent Semantic Index-
ing (LSI) [3]. While efficient, these methods struggle with
vocabulary mismatch across DoDAF viewpoints: Strategic ca-
pabilities are often expressed in high-level business terminol-
ogy, whereas Operational Activities and Services components
employ technical or domain-specific language.
To bridge this semantic divide, domain-adapted Transformer
architectures were introduced. Lin et al. [4] demonstrated that
fine-tuning pre-trained language models via contrastive learn-
ing captures contextual semantics far superior to keyword-
matching baselines. Bonner et al. [5] extended transformer
embeddings to MBSE environments, establishing semantic
links between high-level automotive functional descriptions
and AUTOSAR/SysML design elements. Their work demon-
strated that embedding model metadata alongside textual de-
scriptions significantly reduces false-positive link suggestions
in structured system models.
2) Two-Stage Retrieval and Cross-Encoder Re-ranking:
While bi-encoder embedding models (such as BERT or
Sentence-Transformers) enable rapid candidate retrieval via
vector space similarity, they process source and target artifacts
independently. This independent encoding can fail to capture
fine-grained semantic dependencies between distinct DoDAF
entity types, such as an Operational Activity and a supporting
System Resource.
Information Retrieval research has increasingly adopted
two-stage retrieval-then-reranking architectures to resolve this
limitation [6], [7]. In the first stage, bi-encoder embeddings
retrieve a broad candidate list based on cosine similarity
(rank-by-cosine). In the second stage, a cross-encoder jointly
processes candidate pairs (e.g., Capability vs. Operational
Activity), performing deep cross-attention across both textual
descriptions to refine candidate ordering (rank-by-rerank).
Applying two-stage re-ranking to MBSE model element pairs
provides an efficient mechanism for prioritizing candidate
traceability links prior to human engineering review.
3) LLM-Assisted Model Alignment and Semantic Recovery:
With the advent of generative LLMs, researchers have ex-
plored LLMs for automated architectural analysis and entity
relationship extraction. Fuchß et al. [8] introduced ArTEMiS,
demonstrating that LLMs can extract architectural entities and
candidate relations from unstructured technical documentation.
Similarly, Niu et al. [9] applied Retrieval-Augmented Gener-
ation (RAG) to inject architectural context into LLM prompts
to assist in link identification.
However, existing generative LLM approaches often treat
traceability recovery as a binary classification task or free-
form text generation. In formal MBSE frameworks, systems
engineers require a prioritized, rank-ordered candidate list
constrained by standard IR metrics rather than unconstrained
text outputs.
C. Comparative Evaluation of Existing Approaches
Evaluating the current literature against our MBSE assess-
ment framework reveals key strengths and ongoing limitations
in automated inter-viewpoint mapping:
1) Criterion 1: AI & Retrieval Architecture: Dense vector
retrieval systems [4], [5] provide high scalability for candidate
generation but rely solely on bi-encoder cosine similarity.
These single-stage models struggle to differentiate complex
typed relationships inherent in DoDAF/UAF viewpoints (e.g.,
distinguishing whether a System Resource performs, hosts, or
merely supports an Operational Activity). While RAG and
LLM-assisted pipelines [8], [9] capture richer contextual nu-
ances, they rarely incorporate cross-encoder re-ranking specif-
ically tuned to compare structural model element descriptions
exported from MBSE repositories.
2) Criterion 2: Link Quality & Top-k IR Rigor: Evaluating
link recovery as a top-k recommendation task is critical for
practical systems engineering, as domain experts require prior-
itized candidate lists to minimize manual validation overhead.
Fine-tuned embedding studies (Lin et al. [4], Bonner et al. [5])
demonstrate strong IR evaluation rigor, consistently report-
ing rank-aware metrics such as Precision@k, Recall@k, and
MAP.

distinguishing whether a System Resource performs, hosts, or
merely supports an Operational Activity). While RAG and
LLM-assisted pipelines [8], [9] capture richer contextual nu-
ances, they rarely incorporate cross-encoder re-ranking specif-
ically tuned to compare structural model element descriptions
exported from MBSE repositories.
2) Criterion 2: Link Quality & Top-k IR Rigor: Evaluating
link recovery as a top-k recommendation task is critical for
practical systems engineering, as domain experts require prior-
itized candidate lists to minimize manual validation overhead.
Fine-tuned embedding studies (Lin et al. [4], Bonner et al. [5])
demonstrate strong IR evaluation rigor, consistently report-
ing rank-aware metrics such as Precision@k, Recall@k, and
MAP. In contrast, generative LLM studies (e.g., Eisenreich
et al. [10], Fuchß et al. [8]) frequently report aggregate binary
classification metrics (F1-score, unranked Precision/Recall).
By treating link identification as a binary decision rather
than a ranked recommendation stack, these approaches fail
to quantify human inspection effort across realistic review
budgets (e.g., k = 3).
3) Criterion 3: Architectural Interpretability & Gover-
nance: Classical embedding models operate as numerical
black boxes, outputting similarity scores without semantic
explanation. Generative LLM architectures improve auditabil-
ity by generating step-by-step reasoning or justifications for
suggested links. However, for formal UAF/DoDAF view-
point mapping, deterministic top-k candidate ordering verified
against SME ground truth remains the primary requirement
for airworthiness and enterprise certification audits.
4) Criterion 4: Empirical Validation & MBSE Toolchain
Integration: A major limitation of existing TLR benchmarks is
their heavy reliance on open-source software repositories (e.g.,
Java codebases) or unstructured textual documents. These
benchmarks do not reflect the formal metamodel structures,
concise model element descriptions, or inter-viewpoint de-
pendency networks found in industrial MBSE environments.
Few studies evaluate traceability directly on model elements
extracted from industrial-based repositories containing actual
UAF/DoDAF viewpoints.
D. Summary of Literature Gaps
Our review identifies three primary gaps in the current liter-
ature regarding automated UAF/DoDAF viewpoint mapping:
1) Focus Disparity (Requirements vs. Inter-Viewpoint
Mapping):

2) Lack of Two-Stage Re-ranking in MBSE Traceabil-
ity: Most MBSE link retrieval tools rely exclusively
on single-stage vector embeddings. The combination of
dense embedding retrieval followed by cross-encoder se-
mantic re-ranking has not been systematically evaluated
on model elements defined in different viewpoints.
3) Absence of Rank-Aware Metric Evaluation for Align-
ment: Existing LLM-based architectural mapping stud-
ies often lack rank-aware IR evaluations. There is a
need for empirical benchmarks measuring Precision@k,
Recall@k, MAP, and F1@k at realistic engineering
review cutoffs (k = 3) against SME-established ground
truth.
III. TECHNICAL APPROACH
A. The Positioning, Navigation, and Timing (PNT) Enterprise
Architecture
Positioning, Navigation, and Timing (PNT) data constitute a
foundational utility for modern critical infrastructure, enabling
essential operations across transportation, telecommunications,
energy distribution, finance, and defense. Over the past two
decades, numerous public- and private-sector organizations
have developed PNT architectures, strategic blueprints, and
System-of-Systems (SoS) methodologies to address PNT de-
pendencies, mitigate single points of failure—including un-
mitigated reliance on space-based signals—and coordinate
technology roadmaps across multiple domains [11]–[17].
To evaluate the proposed LLM-driven mapping approach,
this study applies the workflow to a PNT Enterprise Archi-
tecture (EA) developed for a U.S. federal government depart-
ment1. The PNT EA was defined using DoDAF architectural
viewpoints, including the Capability, Operational, and Service
viewpoints. These three viewpoints provide the structured
basis for assessing whether the LLM-assisted workflow can
help systems engineers establish cross-viewpoint relationships
with sufficient semantic fidelity to support enterprise-scale
traceability analysis.

B. The Artificial Intelligence Platform
The experiments reported in this study were conducted on
a secure AIP (Artificial Intelligence Platform). The platform
is designed to operate within a protected environment with
no internet connectivity, preventing data from being shared
with external networks and safeguarding sensitive information
from unauthorized exposure. The AIP provides the following
models for semantic retrieval and ranking that were used in this
study: llama-embed-nemotron 2; llama-nemotron-rerank 3.
A comparative evaluation of embedding and re-ranking models
is beyond the scope of this paper. Readers are referred to [18],
[19] for comparisons of embedding models and to [20] for
comparisons of re-ranking models.
C. AI-Assisted Semantic Traceability Workflow
As illustrated in Figure 1, the proposed workflow comprises
six stages that support the establishment of candidate trace-
ability links between UAF/DoDAF architectural viewpoints.
The workflow transforms these viewpoints into dense semantic
embeddings. Embedding-based retrieval and cross-encoder re-
ranking are then used to identify and prioritize candidate trace-
ability links. Validation activities are incorporated through-
out the workflow, enabling a systematic assessment of both
computational behavior and traceability effectiveness within a
unified methodological framework.
a) Step 1 – Extraction of DoDAF Architectural view-
points: The workflow begins by exporting architectural view-
points from the Cameo Systems Modeler repository. In this
case study, the following DoDAF viewpoints were addressed:
• Capability viewpoint containing enterprise capabilities,
their interdependencies, and business drivers.
• Operational viewpoint containing the enterprise opera-
tional activities and performers.
• Service viewpoint containing the services and their inter-
connections supporting or providing the PNT functions.
DoDAF obviously contains many other viewpoints. However,
the case study analyzed in this report at the time this study was
conducted had a limited set of DoDAF viewpoints defined.
b) Step 2 – Semantic Embedding Generation: Model
elements along their documentation exported from Cameo are
converted into dense semantic vector representations using
the AIP’s embedding model. Each model element, such as
a capability, is represented by a single embedding vector.
c) Step 3 – Candidate Trace Retrieval: For each source
model element, e.g., capability, cosine similarity is computed
between its embedding vector and the embeddings of all target
model elements, e.g., operational activities. This produces an

denoted rank-by-rerank, improves the ordering of semantically

based retrieval.

d) Step 4 – Cross-Encoder Re-ranking: To refine can-
didate prioritization, the top-3 DoDAF architectural view-
points retrieved by the embedding-based retrieval stage are re-
evaluated using a cross-encoder. Whereas embedding models
represent artifacts independently, the cross-encoder jointly
analyzes pairs of potential mapping, such as capability vs

denoted rank-by-rerank, improves the ordering of semantically
similar candidates while retaining the efficiency of embedding-
based retrieval. As reported by [6], [7], retrieval-then-reranking
architectures have become increasingly common in informa-
tion retrieval systems because they enable efficient candidate
retrieval followed by a more detailed relevance assessment.
e) Step 5 – Subject Matter Expert Validation: The ranked
candidate traceability links are reviewed by a SME. For
each proposed link, the SME examines the source and target
architectural elements, along with any available supporting
documentation, to assess the validity of the cross-viewpoint
relationship. For example, when mapping capabilities to opera-
tional activities, the SME evaluates whether each candidate ac-
tivity supports the source capability. This validation approach
is applied consistently across all mapping types evaluated in
the study. Each candidate link is classified as:
• Accepted: the target element adequately supports or
realizes the intent of the source element.
• Partially Accepted: the target element supports or real-
izes only part of the intent of the source element.
• Rejected: the target element does not provide a mean-
ingful traceability relationship to the source element.
The resulting SME judgments constitute the reference trace-
ability baseline used to evaluate the candidate rankings and the
effectiveness of the proposed workflow.
f) Step 6 – Retrieval Performance Evaluation: The ef-
fectiveness of the workflow is assessed by comparing the
automatically generated rankings against the SME baseline
using standard Information Retrieval (IR) metrics as defined
in Table I.

workflow consistently surfaces relevant target model elements

• Capability-to-Operational Activity (CV-6): Achieving

successfully aggregates the relevant functional cluster,
SME validation remains necessary to distinguish primary

• Operational Activity-to-Service (SvcV-5): Tracing ab-
stract operational workflows (OV-5a) to technical service
implementations (SvcV-1) yields high candidate recovery
(Success@3 = 0.950)[cite: 16]. Unlike capability-level
mappings, Cross-Encoder Reranking provides a distinct
advantage here, increasing the Top-1 Acceptance Rate
from 0.863 to 0.900 and MRR@3 from 0.902 to 0.925.
Because services rely on specialized interface terminol-
ogy, the cross-encoder’s deep attention mechanism effec-
tively resolves cross-viewpoint vocabulary mismatches to
place the primary service first 90% of the time. Further-
more, the Precision@3 drop from Rule 1 (0.725) to Rule
2 (0.477) reflects service-oriented modularity: individual
services rarely fulfill an operational activity in isolation,
requiring SME verification of service composability and
orchestration.

vs. 0.910) by capturing global semantic intent with-

B. Strategy Comparison: Cosine vs. Cross-Encoder Reranking
To determine whether the reranking provides a statisti-
cally meaningful improvement over single-stage bi-encoder
retrieval, paired hypothesis tests were performed for each met-
ric across input types and relevance rules. Top-1 Acceptance
Rate and Success@3 were evaluated using McNemar’s test
for paired nominal data, while MRR@3 and Precision@3
were evaluated using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test for paired
continuous/ordinal distributions.
The paired comparisons confirm that Cosine similarity and
Cross-Encoder Reranking exhibit statistically indistinguishable
performance across all tasks and metrics (p > 0.05):
• For operational-to-service mapping, reranking increases
Top-1 Acceptance Rate by 3.7% (0.863 to 0.900) and
MRR@3 by 0.023 (0.902 to 0.925), though these im-
provements do not reach statistical significance (p =
0.4531 and p = 0.2500, respectively).
• For capability-based mappings, Cosine similarity slightly
outperforms Reranking at Top-1 (0.846 vs. 0.821 for
capability-to-operational activity; 0.872
vs. 0.846 for capability-to-service), but these
differences are statistically non-significant (p = 1.0000).
• Precision@3 and Success@3 values are identical be-
tween Cosine and Rerank across all inputs and rules
(p = 1.0000). Because the cross-encoder only reorders
the top three candidate items retrieved during the initial
vector search, candidate set membership remains un-
changed, resulting in identical set-based precision and
recall boundaries.
C. Impact of Relevance Scoring Rules
To evaluate how strict acceptance criteria affect engineering
review quality, Precision@3 was compared between Rule 1
(inclusive relevance) and Rule 2 (strict/weighted relevance)
using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test.
The transition from Rule 1 to Rule 2 results in a statistically
significant reduction in Precision@3 across all architectural
mapping types (p = 0.0002):

This significant drop demonstrates that while the workflow
consistently presents candidates that are at least partially rele-
vant (Rule 1), a substantial fraction of top-3 recommendations
correspond to partial realizations or overlapping functional
coverage rather than complete realization. These findings
highlight the essential role of SME oversight in validating
enterprise architecture traceability: while AI-driven semantic
retrieval effectively identifies relevant candidate links, human
inspection remains necessary to distinguish full realization
from partial functional alignment.
D. Key Takeaways for Systems Engineering Practice
1) Semantic Retrieval Can Support Initial Traceability
Candidate Discovery: Manual establishment and re-
view of cross-viewpoint traceability can require substan-
tial systems engineering effort, particularly as enterprise
architectures become larger and more interconnected. In
the evaluated PNT case study, the workflow achieved
Success@3 ≥0.950 across all three mapping tasks, indi-
cating that relevant candidate relationships were consis-
tently present within the top-3 recommendations. These
results suggest that semantic retrieval can support the
initial discovery of traceability candidates and provide a
bounded set of relationships for subsequent SME review.
The study did not directly measure reductions in review
time or the elimination of orphaned architectural ele-
ments; such effects therefore require further evaluation.
2) Cross-Encoder Re-ranking Did Not Produce a Sta-

evaluated case study, paired statistical tests found no
statistically significant differences between cosine-based
retrieval and cross-encoder re-ranking across the re-

from 0.902 to 0.925 for Operational Activity-to-Service
mapping, but these differences were not statistically sig-
nificant.

architectural elements may have partial or overlapping

prioritizes candidate relationships for engineering review
rather than as an autonomous traceability classifier. SME
assessment remains necessary in the evaluated workflow
to distinguish accepted relationships from partial or
rejected mappings.
V. CONCLUSION
This study investigated an LLM-assisted semantic trace-
ability workflow for establishing mappings across DoDAF
architectural viewpoints. The proposed approach combines
dense semantic embedding retrieval with cross-encoder re-
ranking and evaluates the resulting candidate rankings against
SME judgments using rank-aware Information Retrieval met-
rics. The workflow was evaluated using a real-world PNT
Enterprise Architecture containing Capability, Operational,
and Service viewpoints, providing an empirical setting for
examining automated cross-viewpoint mapping in an MBSE
context.
Across the three mapping tasks evaluated—Capability-
to-Operational Activity, Operational Activity-to-Service, and
Capability-to-Service—the workflow consistently identified
relevant candidates within a top-3 review budget. Success@3
was 1.000 for the Capability-to-Operational Activity and
Capability-to-Service mappings and 0.950 for Operational
Activity-to-Service. These results indicate that semantic re-
trieval can provide high-yield candidate sets for SME re-
view across the evaluated viewpoints. At the same time,
the reduction in Precision@3 under the stricter 2-1-0 rele-
vance rule demonstrates that semantic similarity does not, by
itself, reliably distinguish complete realization from partial
or overlapping functional relationships. The SME therefore
remains an important component of the traceability process,
particularly where architectural relationships involve multiple
complementary elements.
The comparison between cosine-based retrieval and cross-
encoder re-ranking also provides a more nuanced result than
a simple preference for the more complex retrieval strategy.
Although re-ranking improved Top-1 Acceptance Rate and
MRR@3 for Operational Activity-to-Service mapping, the
observed differences were not statistically significant. For the
two capability-oriented mappings, cosine retrieval produced
slightly higher Top-1 and MRR@3 values, also without statis-
tically significant differences. Because re-ranking was applied
only to candidates already retrieved in the initial top-3 set, the
two methods produced identical Success@3 and Precision@3
values. Within the scope of this case study, these results
therefore do not establish a general performance advantage for
cross-encoder re-ranking over single-stage semantic retrieval.
The primary implication for systems engineering practice
is that LLM-based semantic retrieval can serve as a practical
decision-support mechanism for cross-viewpoint traceability,
while responsibility for accepting and interpreting architectural
relationships remains with systems engineering experts. The
results further suggest that the value of such workflows should
be assessed not only by whether they retrieve semantically
related elements, but also by how well they support engineers
in distinguishing fully realized relationships from partial or
supporting relationships.

Building upon the findings of this study several key avenues
for future investigation emerge:
1) Expanded DoDAF Viewpoint and Metamodel Cover-
age: Future work will extend the semantic workflow to
additional DoDAF or UAF viewpoints and incorporate
structural metamodel constraints directly into the candi-
date retrieval process to prevent semantically plausible
but structurally invalid mappings.
2) Expanded Coverage Across Enterprise Architec-
tures: While this study focuses on a single PNT EA, fu-
ture work should extend the workflow to support cross-
enterprise and cross-organizational mapping, facilitating
model reuse, cross-domain interoperability, and broader
architectural alignment.
3) Direct
Cameo
Toolchain
Integration: To further
streamline systems engineering workflows, future efforts
will focus on embedding the two-stage AI retrieval
pipeline into open-source Cameo Systems Modeler plu-
gins, enabling automated, real-time traceability checks
directly inside the modeling environment.
4) Fine-Tuning on Domain-Specific Systems Engineer-
ing Corpora: Investigating parameter-efficient fine-
tuning (PEFT) on specialized defense, aerospace, and
MBSE datasets may further refine cross-encoder re-
ranking accuracy across domain-specific jargon and
technical abbreviations.
Finally, it is important to point out that this study is
limited to a single PNT Enterprise Architecture, three DoDAF
viewpoints, the selected embedding and re-ranking models
available on the secure Artificial Intelligence Platform, and
validation based on SME judgments. Accordingly, the findings
should be interpreted as evidence from an industrial case study
rather than as a general demonstration of LLM-based traceabil-
ity across all enterprise architectures or MBSE frameworks.
